claims.text: The target quaternary equiatomic alloy has an FCC structure.
The target alloy contains significant short-range order.
The target alloy has high lattice distortion.
Yielding at low temperature is dislocation-based.
Above approximately 0.5 Tm, yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate.
The proposed strain-rate insensitivity is caused by saturation of SRO drag on edge dislocations.
The dominant deformation mechanism shifts from thermally activated dislocation glide to athermal phase transformation or twinning at elevated temperature.
SRO clusters act as drag centers for edge dislocations.
An FCC-to-HCP or other phase-transformation barrier is a relevant structural mediator in the target alloy.
At low temperature, SRO impedes dislocation glide and produces strong thermally activated strain-rate dependence.
Increasing temperature supplies sufficient thermal energy to overcome the SRO drag barrier.
After SRO drag is overcome, phase-transformation or twinning nucleation becomes rate-limiting.
Phase transformation or twinning is less strain-rate-sensitive than dislocation glide in the proposed temperature regime.
At intermediate-to-high temperature, the strain-rate-sensitivity exponent will plateau and yield strength will remain constant as strain rate increases.
At low temperature, yield strength has a strong positive correlation with strain rate.
Standard dislocation-glide theory predicts continuously increasing yield strength with strain rate at all temperatures in FCC metals unless phase transformation occurs.
The proposed plateau requires SRO to be the primary strengthening mechanism and the FCC phase to be metastable enough to transform under the test conditions.
A characteristic SRO influence length of approximately 1.2 nm has been observed.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis locates strain-rate insensitivity above 0.5 Tm, whereas the proposed experiment treats exactly 0.5 Tm as the predicted plateau temperature.
A plateau in the exponent m does not necessarily mean strain-rate-insensitive or constant yield strength; a constant nonzero m still implies continuing strain-rate dependence.
